introduction: These hundred passages are letters and words of comfort: to the bereaved, the exiled, the unemployed, the slandered and the lonely. They say that God is the companion of the solitary, that the dead are freed birds whose happiness is touched by ours, that hardship passes, and that friends must become each other's consolers. Beside them stand a hundred voices from other scriptures and from poets and letter-writers who have tried to comfort, or who found that they could not be comforted: the Psalms and Job, the Gospels and Paul, the Qur’an, Epictetus and Seneca, Shakespeare, Donne, Tennyson, Dickinson and Lincoln.
questions: Several letters ask the bereaved not to weep, because mourning distresses the departed; John's Gospel shows Jesus weeping and Confucius defends his own tears. How do you hold these together?
One letter says in advance that whatever the reader complains of is right. What does the book of Job suggest about why consolation might begin there?
Many passages promise that hardship does not last. What can be said to someone who, like Job, cannot yet believe it?
The friends are told to become each other's consolers. Which of the outside voices shows best what a consoling word or act looks like?
Separation is called the essence of union here, and Donne calls parting an expansion. When has absence deepened a bond in your experience?
One letter recommends composing a poem when melancholy comes. What do Shakespeare and Tennyson add about what words can and cannot do for grief?

outside.why: The letter to the Hebrews also grounds comfort in a comforter who has himself been wronged, tried and a stranger.
The psalmist gives sorrow one night and joy the morning, the same order of things that this passage promises.
A psalm names the same Lord by the same work: healing the broken in heart and binding up their wounds.
The last words of Matthew's Gospel make the same promise of a presence that does not depend on being seen.
Isaiah hears the same assurance for the exile: through water and fire, the traveller is not left alone.
Isaiah says of God what this letter says of its writer: that the sorrow of the afflicted was felt as his own.
Dickinson also pictures an early death as a courteous journey rather than an ending, though she leaves the destination unstated. What does the image of the nest add to hers?
David stops weeping when his child dies, and gives a reason close to this one: the living will go to the dead, not the dead return.
Here the mourner is asked not to weep. In John's Gospel Jesus weeps at a grave he is about to open. Is there a grief that is no failure of faith?
Paul writes to a bereaved community in the same spirit: grieve, but not as those who have no hope.
Seneca, writing to a friend, calls the dreaded last day the birthday of eternity, a Stoic kinship with this view of the soul.
This is the verse of the Qur’an that the letter quotes, in its own setting of trial, loss and patience.
Tennyson, mourning a friend, holds that the pain of loss is the price of having loved and is worth paying. Does that thought console differently from the promise of reunion?
Paul sums up a faithful life as a course finished and a faith kept, the consolation this letter draws from a mother's long constancy.
Epictetus teaches the bereaved the same change of words: not "I have lost" but "I have given back."
The Gospel of John consoles with the same assurance of a place prepared and a meeting to come.
The Qur’an speaks of death as a passage into a form of life that the living cannot yet picture.
A president writing to a mother of fallen sons admits how weak words are, and still offers the pride that belongs to such a sacrifice.
Rossetti gives the departed the same wish this passage gives them: that those left behind be happy rather than sad in remembering.
Constance, told she is too fond of grief, answers that grief is all she has left of her child. What would this letter say to her?
A psalm uses the same picture of release: the soul as a bird escaped from the fowler's broken snare.
The psalmist also trusts that sorrow is written down in a book kept by God, and takes comfort from that record.
Confucius, reproached for excessive mourning of a beloved disciple, asks for whom he should mourn if not for this man. Can restraint in grief be asked of everyone?
Jesus tells his disciples that their present sorrow will be turned into a joy no one can take from them.
In John's Gospel too the departure of the teacher is presented as a gain for those who remain, not an extinction.
Job's first words after his losses are a near relation of the verse quoted here: what was given has been taken back by the giver.
Lear over Cordelia's body finds no patience and no return, only "never." The passage itself lets a cry against death stand beside its resignation. Why keep both?
Paul asks the same fellowship of feeling: to weep with those who weep, as this passage says the lovers have done.
Paul makes the mutual carrying of burdens the fulfilment of the law, as this passage makes it a duty of friends.
The Gospel likewise counts the smallest act of care for another as something noticed and rewarded by God.
Peter too has no money to give and says so, then offers what he does have. The embarrassment here is of the same honest kind.
The prophet Habakkuk rejoices with empty stalls and failed harvests, the same refusal to let want decide the heart's state.
Paul's counsel for anxiety is the same pair this passage names: prayer and a peace that comes from resignation.
A psalm declares the same confidence when the earth itself gives way: help is found when every other hope has gone.
Carlyle's remedy for a troubled mind is also work: do the duty that lies nearest, and the next will become clear.
The Qur’an states in one line what this letter tells a man out of work: ease accompanies hardship.
Job in his suffering sees his days running out without hope and expects no return of good. What can be said to someone who cannot yet believe that hardship ends?
The Qur’an gives the reasoning behind "perhaps God will bring about something": what is disliked may prove to be good.
The Qur’an promises a way out and provision from an unexpected quarter, the same confidence offered to this traveller.
Longfellow reminds a sad heart that its fate is the common one and that the sun still shines behind the cloud.
Isaiah promises those without children a name better than sons and daughters, a like answer to the same grief.
The exiles by Babylon's rivers cannot sing; their hardship is not easy to bear. Does the example of a greater exile lighten one's own, or only shame it?
At the end of the book of Job, God says the complainer spoke rightly and his correct friends did not. How does that verdict bear on this promise to accept every complaint?
A poet writing from prison makes the same turn: confinement of the body is not the prison that matters.
In the middle of Lamentations hope returns in the same way, as mercy that is new every morning.
Dickinson describes hope as a bird that keeps singing through the storm, a picture for the dawn this letter reports.
The Preacher holds that sorrow improves the heart and that the house of mourning teaches more than the house of feasting.
The letter of James asks the same hard thing: to count trials as joy for what they produce.
Ivan Karamazov refuses any harmony bought with suffering and returns his ticket. Is thanksgiving for affliction possible for one's own suffering only, and not for another's?
Paul describes the same chain: those comforted in their trouble become able to comfort others in theirs.
This is the verse of the Qur’an that the passage echoes: the patient are paid their wages without measure.
The letter of James also points the suffering to patience and to the end that was given to Job.
Epictetus gives the Stoic form of patience with what is decreed: wish things to happen as they do.
Job's friends argue that he must be in the wrong, and he calls them miserable comforters. This letter begins by granting the complaint. Why might consolation need to start there?
The psalmist turns in the same direction when human loyalties fail: if father and mother forsake, the Lord takes up.
Paul records the same experience without bitterness: all forsook him, and yet he was not left alone.
Elijah under the juniper tree asks to die; the story answers with food, sleep and a further task. What does that reply add to this letter's astonishment?
The Qur’an recalls the Prophet's words to his companion in the cave: do not grieve, for God is with us.
The letter to the Hebrews honours the persecuted and their families in the same way, as those of whom the world was not worthy.
Jesus also speaks of his suffering as a cup that his followers will be given to share.
Jesus on the way to execution tells the women not to weep for him. This letter says there is no harm in such sorrow. When is grief for another's suffering to be welcomed?
The Revelation of John ends with the same promise that former sorrows will pass and be forgotten.
Paul weighs present trouble as light and momentary against what is to come, as this letter does.
The Sermon on the Mount blesses the reviled and places them in the company of earlier sufferers, as this advice does.
Paul gives the same rule for answering injury: feed the enemy, and overcome evil with good.
Joseph, wronged by his brothers, refuses blame and sees a larger purpose, the spirit this letter asks toward a brother.
A psalm tells the oppressed not to fret over evildoers, for their power is as brief as cut grass.
Jesus gives his followers the same encouragement in the face of the world's hostility: be of good cheer.
Paul, writing from prison, says he has learned contentment in every state, a companion to this refusal to complain.
The psalm that Jesus quotes on the cross is an open complaint to God. Do contentment with the decree and a cry of abandonment belong to different moments, or to the same faith?
The Gospel gives the same assurance of constant care: not a sparrow falls unnoticed, and you are worth more.
Proverbs observes how much a single good word does for a heavy heart, as her friends tried to tell her.
Jesus points his disciples to the same ground of joy: that their names are written in heaven.
Isaiah answers the fear of being overlooked with a name engraved on the palms of God's hands.
Paul writes to absent friends in the same tone: parted in presence, never in heart.
Augustine opens his Confessions with the same finding: no rest for the heart until it rests in God.
Hopkins tells a grieving child that all sorrows have one spring, the human lot itself. Does naming grief as universal comfort, or does it need the turn toward God that this talk adds?
Emerson, after his son's death, confesses that grief taught him nothing and left him untouched in his depths. What would it take for sorrow to become a source of solace?
The elder of the third letter of John opens with the same affectionate wish for a friend's health.
Paul thanks God at every remembrance of distant friends, the same happiness in thinking of the absent.
Donne tells his wife that their parting is no breach but an expansion, like gold beaten thin. How close is a lover's reasoning to this account of separation as union?
A psalm confesses the same accompaniment in every going and coming: there is no place beyond that presence.
The psalmist speaks to his own downcast soul as this passage speaks to its reader, and bids it hope.
A saying of Muhammad holds that deeds are rewarded by their intentions, which is why the hindered pilgrim loses nothing.
A psalm of pilgrimage voices the longing itself, envying the sparrow that nests at the altar. Is such longing a lack to be consoled, or already a kind of arrival?
Paul lists his own journeys by land and sea with their dangers, a fellow wanderer for the sake of his message.
Paul makes the same claim to his distant readers: absent in body, with them in spirit.
The Preacher's best-known lines say the same: to every thing there is a season and a time.
A psalm affirms what this prayer asks: that God is near to the broken-hearted in their affliction.
A psalm praises God in the terms of this prayer: father of the fatherless, who sets the solitary in families.
Isaiah takes a mother's comforting as the image of God's own, fitting a prayer for a bereaved mother.
Dickinson measures a life the same way: it is not in vain if it has stopped one heart from breaking.
Isaiah's servant is given a trained tongue for one purpose, to speak a timely word to the weary.
The letter of James also prescribes prayer and song for the changing states of the heart.
Shakespeare's Malcolm urges a bereaved man to give his sorrow words lest it break the heart. This letter recommends words of praise instead. What does each kind of utterance do for grief?
Tennyson doubts his own elegy: verse numbs pain like a narcotic and half conceals what it tells. Can composing a poem transform sorrow, or does it only dull it?
The elder of John's letters has the same joy amid his cares: hearing that those he loves walk in truth.
Isaiah receives the same commission on behalf of another: comfort my people, and speak tenderly to them.
This is the verse of the Qur’an, spoken by Jacob about his lost sons, whose words this passage takes up.
Arnold on Dover beach hears faith withdrawing from the world and expects no return of the tide. On what does this passage rest its opposite expectation?

psalm-very-present-help.text: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea

kings-it-is-enough.text: But he himself went a day's journey into the wilderness, and came and sat down under a juniper tree: and he requested for himself that he might die; and said, It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers

timothy-all-men-forsook-me.text: At my first answer no man stood with me, but all men forsook me: I pray God that it may not be laid to their charge. Notwithstanding the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me

psalm-fret-not-thyself.text: Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity. For they shall soon be cut down like the grass, and wither as the green herb

proverbs-good-word-maketh-it-glad.text: Heaviness in the heart of man maketh it stoop: but a good word maketh it glad

proverbs-merry-heart.text: A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones

isaiah-word-in-season-to-the-weary.text: The Lord God hath given me the tongue of the learned, that I should know how to speak a word in season to him that is weary: he wakeneth morning by morning, he wakeneth mine ear to hear as the learned

psalm-why-art-thou-cast-down.text: Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance

james-let-him-sing-psalms.text: Is any among you afflicted? let him pray. Is any merry? let him sing psalms

john-sorrow-turned-into-joy.text: Verily, verily, I say unto you, That ye shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice: and ye shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy. A woman when she is in travail hath sorrow, because her hour is come: but as soon as she is delivered of the child, she remembereth no more the anguish, for joy that a man is born into the world. And ye now therefore have sorrow: but I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man taketh from you

quran-with-hardship-goeth-ease.text: But lo! with hardship goeth ease,

quran-paid-without-stint.text: Say: O My bondmen who believe! Observe your duty to your Lord. For those who do good in this world there is good, and Allah's earth is spacious. Verily the steadfast will be paid their wages without stint.

quran-despair-not-of-the-spirit.text: Go, O my sons, and ascertain concerning Joseph and his brother, and despair not of the Spirit of Allah. Lo! none despaireth of the Spirit of Allah save disbelieving folk.

rossetti-forget-and-smile.text: Better by far you should forget and smile / Than that you should remember and be sad
rossetti-forget-and-smile.author: Christina Rossetti

donne-not-a-breach-but-an-expansion.text: Our two souls therefore, which are one, / Though I must go, endure not yet / A breach, but an expansion, / Like gold to airy thinness beat
donne-not-a-breach-but-an-expansion.author: John Donne

dickinson-thing-with-feathers.text: Hope is the thing with feathers / That perches in the soul, / And sings the tune without the words, / And never stops at all
dickinson-thing-with-feathers.author: Emily Dickinson

lincoln-bixby-letter.text: I feel how weak and fruitless must be any words of mine which should attempt to beguile you from the grief of a loss so overwhelming. But I cannot refrain from tendering to you the consolation that may be found in the thanks of the Republic they died to save
lincoln-bixby-letter.author: Abraham Lincoln

psalm-nigh-unto-broken-heart.text: The Lord is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit. Many are the afflictions of the righteous: but the Lord delivereth him out of them all

job-days-are-swifter.text: My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and are spent without hope. O remember that my life is wind: mine eye shall no more see good

ecclesiastes-house-of-mourning.text: It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living will lay it to his heart. Sorrow is better than laughter: for by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better

john-epistle-prosper-and-be-in-health.text: Beloved, I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth

thessalonians-in-presence-not-in-heart.text: But we, brethren, being taken from you for a short time in presence, not in heart, endeavoured the more abundantly to see your face with great desire

psalm-longeth-for-the-courts.text: My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the Lord: my heart and my flesh crieth out for the living God. Yea, the sparrow hath found an house, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, even thine altars, O Lord of hosts, my King, and my God
